newsitem.title: UK: Markets set for UK rate rise but 1/2% would shock.
newsitem.headline: Markets set for UK rate rise but 1/2% would shock.

text.p: Britain's financial markets are resigned to the prospect of an interest rate rise this week -- rarely has a monetary tightening been more widely expected.
But experienced market-watchers get twitchy when the vast majority of players are positioned one way.

The Bank of England's monetary policy committee, now empowered to set interest rates, meets this week and will signal its decision on rates at midday on Thursday. The market consensus is firmly set on a quarter-point hike.

But after two rate rises in the past two months, there has to be a chance the Bank will hold fire, adopting the tactics of its German counterpart, the Bundesbank, which delights in catching markets on the hop.

Alternatively, it could opt for a more aggressive, half-point increase to ward off the inflationary threat offered by unrestrained high-street spending. Either would be a surprise and either is quite possible.
"We're looking for a quarter-point rise on Thursday," David Bloom, UK economist at HSBC James Capel, said. "The Bank will take sterling's rise on board but will still go for a cautious increase."

Anything else could be taken badly by the stock and gilts markets. "To leave rates on hold would be seen by the markets as a policy error while a half-point rate rise would signal the Bank's unhappiness with the budget and lead to further turmoil," Bloom said.

At the moment, the flat yield curve shows the gilt market believes the Bank will keep long-term inflation under control. That credibility would be threatened if the committee does not move rates this time.

Financial analysts 4CAST polled 75 contributors from dealing desks around Europe and found 67 expected the Bank's monetary policy committee to raise rates on Thursday, an unusually high level of consensus. Of those, 61 expected a quarter-point rise, taking base rates to 6.75 percent. Six forecast a half-point increase.

Interest rate futures are certainly positioned for another round of tightening. The September short sterling future, which has dropped about 20 basis points since Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget last week, is implying rates at seven percent by the end of September.

Brown's budget did much to harden interest rate expectations. Although it introduced a package of tax rises which will take nearly 6 billion pounds ($10 billion) out of the economy, little of that was aimed at consumer spending.

Britain's big stores are experiencing near-boom conditions as consumers spend freely, partly in eager anticipation of more than 30 billion pounds in windfalls from building societies as they convert into banks.

Inflation data out on Tuesday did little to ease rate rise fears. Underlying inflation, which excludes volatile home loan payments, rose to 2.7 percent in June, above the government's 2.5 target which it had been expected to meet.
But much of the rise in prices was due to a five percent monthly increase in notoriously volatile seasonal food prices. They were forced up as heavy rain in June soaked crops across Europe.

"The market's nervousness about this week's meeting is understandable but setting interest rates according to the weather might be stretching the bearishness a little too far," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
Falls in the price of clothing and footwear and household goods in June, which should continue as the summer sales season kicks in, suggests the real picture was much more benign, he said.
But Bloom said seasonal food prices, which are still seven percent lower than they were a year ago regardless of June's rise, are still taking a chunk off the year-on-year RPI.
"That can't happen forever. We could see RPIX at three percent before we know it," he said.
There are powerful lobbies in British industry pleading for the Bank to hold off for now.
Figures out on Monday showed manufacturing output slumped by 1.1 percent in June, the largest monthly fall in four years.
Economists said that offered clear evidence that the super-strong pound, up more than 20 percent since last August, is pushing up export prices and cutting orders.
Another rate rise will simply push the pound higher still, and while it will restrain domestic demand to some extent, it will also make conditions even tougher for British industry.
Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, agreed with Bloom that the level of the pound would restrict the Bank to a quarter-point tightening this week.

"The mix of the high pound, a modest further rise in base rates and the tight fiscal plans -- even allowing for the limited impact on growth of the budget itself -- constitutes a heavy squeeze on growth."

The Engineering Employers' Federation added its voice to the chorus of hard-pressed manufacturers on Tuesday. It said engineering export orders plunged to their lowest level for three years in the second quarter, as the pound's strength bit.
But the Bank is likely to remain unmoved by those pleas, fulfilling its mandate to temper the inflation outlook two years out.

"The Bank is looking at inflation in 12-18 months time and those pressures are coming from the services sector and not manufacturing," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident. ($ = 0.594 British Pounds)
